title: Baba Dayal's Nirankaris today
hookLine: a reform movement distinct from the later Sant Nirankari Mission

cards: Two restaurants in one city share a name. One is a family place that has served the same dish for generations. The other opened later, with a different menu and a different owner.
Locals never mix them up. Visitors do it all the time, and the family place keeps having to explain: that's not us. Sikh history has a pair like that.
Two movements carry the word Nirankari. They are not the same, and today is about telling them apart, carefully and fairly.

teach.b: Start with the word. Nirankar means the Formless One, a name for God that runs through Gurbani.
In the Japji, from Ang 3, Guru Nanak closes several stanzas with a refrain, in paraphrase: you are forever safe and whole, O Formless One. To be a Nirankari is to belong to the Formless.

teach.h: BABA DAYAL: BACK TO THE FORMLESS.
teach.b: The first movement: Baba Dayal was a Sikh reformer in the northwest of Punjab, in the city of Rawalpindi.
Tradition remembers him calling Sikhs back to the Formless One and away from rites he saw creeping in: idols, priestly ceremonies, customs that pulled attention from the Guru's word.
His movement is especially remembered for weddings.
Nirankaris married by circling the Guru Granth Sahib while the Lavan, Guru Ram Das's wedding hymns, were sung: the anand karaj, the wedding rite Sikhs know today.
Baba Dayal's Nirankaris continue as a community that honors the Guru Granth Sahib and remembers its founder.

The second movement: the Sant Nirankari Mission is a later and separate organization, with its own living leaders and its own teachings. Sikh bodies have been in serious, painful disagreement with it.
That story is heavy and deserves more than one sentence in a short lesson, so this path leaves it there.
Why the distinction matters: when the two are confused, a reform remembered for the wedding around the Granth gets tangled up with a conflict it had no part in.
Knowing the difference is a small act of fairness to both.

how: Sikhs distinguish Baba Dayal's Nirankari reform, remembered for calling Sikhs to the Formless One and for weddings around the Guru Granth Sahib, from the later and separate Sant Nirankari Mission.

games.q: what does “baba dayal's nirankaris today” mean?
o: the later mission with its own living leaders
a group that brought idols into the gurdwara
a reform that called Sikhs back to the Formless One

games.q: inside know the difference: tap the pairs.
p: marriage around the Guru Granth Sahib

s: Baba Dayal's Nirankaris and the Sant Nirankari Mission are the same movement
they share a word, not a story. the mission is later and separate.
Baba Dayal's movement is remembered for weddings around the Guru Granth Sahib
couples circled the Granth while the Lavan were sung: the anand karaj.
Nirankar is a name for God found in Gurbani
the Japji's refrain addresses the Formless One.

games.q: a friend reads a headline about a conflict with 'the Nirankaris' and asks if that's Baba Dayal's reform. what's the fair answer?
o: no; the Sant Nirankari Mission is a later, separate movement.
games.why: Baba Dayal's reform and the Sant Nirankari Mission are distinct. mixing them up tangles a reform in a conflict it had no part in.

practice: Say the two names to yourself once, slowly, and attach one plain fact to each: Baba Dayal's Nirankaris, the reformer and the wedding around the Granth; the Sant Nirankari Mission, later and separate.
Breathe in on the first, out on the second, and let them sit apart like two houses on different streets. If you pray, rest on Nirankar, the Formless One.

wordCard.voice: Baba Dayal's Nirankaris today. A reform movement that called Sikhs back to the Formless One and is remembered for weddings around the Granth. Separate from the later Sant Nirankari Mission. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: one who belongs to Nirankar, the Formless One.

carryVoice: Your line: know the difference. Two names alike can belong to very different stories. Go gently.

sources.ref: Ang 773–774 (Lavan, Raag Suhi, Guru Ram Das)
